title.narrative: We Cannot Wait Towards an Inclusive and Diverse Women's Movement in the GHoA

description.narrative: In Ethiopia, EWLA will target individuals as well as groups of disadvantaged or poor women and girls of all ages ranging from secondary school to university, government officials (both men and women), members of the parliament (both men and women), and women politicians. These target individuals and groups will be approached at the national, regional and community levels urban and rural areas as per EWLA’s structure. These stakeholders will be approached based on EWLA’s record of work and previous and ongoing assessments. Stakeholders also may lack awareness on gender equality, have negligence on promoting and realisation of women rights and be constrained by budgetary needs.

The "We Cannot Wait: towards an inclusive and diverse women’s movement in the Greater Horn of Africa project represents an entirely Southern-led consortium of organizations that are explicitly focused on women’s empowerment throughout the Greater Horn of Africa (GHoA). The consortium works in the following countries: Somalia, Uganda, Sudan, South Sudan, and Ethiopia.
The project aims at strengthening women’s leadership and participation in (political) decision-making and strengthening women’s economic empowerment and improving the economic climate for women's participation. The project is targeted at women's rights activists and organizations. Project strategies include capacity building for effective advocacy, linking women's rights activists and organizations for a common agenda and action, and improving their access to advocacy platforms are among the project's tactics.
Women in the Greater Horn of Africa will be leading and defining the political, sociocultural and economic agenda through a gender lens at all levels

title.narrative: WRGE 5.2.1 - WROs have strengthened advocacy and lobbying skills

description.narrative: EWLA has been using art to educate the public. One of its well-known ventures was 'Berchi,' which included both print and theatre media. EWLA believes in the great power of art as a tool for raising awareness about many concerns. Participants were invited because EWLA believes in their power in the art world and is eager to collaborate with them to address women's rights and stereotypes Workshop. And provide gender equality training to raise awareness of the importance of recognizing and defending the dignity of women's rights as well as the rights of all people for participants from various stakeholder offices such as CSOs, government offices, and judges to build their capabilities for voice and influence. The experience of group cohesiveness and solidarity may contribute to individual and collective self-affirmation, provide support and legitimacy to gender equality agendas, and enable women to exercise the collective power required to transform gender norms.

title.narrative: Creating an enabling environment will be created through a variety of approaches, including the formation of strong coalitions, strategic negotiation with government at all levels, influencing at regional and international levels, and directly addressing discriminatory norms and practices through informed dialogue and campaigns. Based on this, EWLA held a consolation workshop on women's rights advocacy and established networking with female judges, female public prosecutors, and female attorneys to understand the specific challenges of the legal framework and practice. Participants in this consultation session are change agents, and advocates and lobbyists will be able to use these skills and tools to push for continuous social transformational processes. Women's capacity to pursue community leadership positions will also be increased.

description.narrative: Youth-led organizations have strengthened capacity to advance women's rights and gender equality

comment.narrative:
In Ethiopia, Women Rights Organizations have played a pivotal role in advancing the GEWE agenda, with organizations such as EWLA having a track record of researching GBV issues and identifying the gaps in legislation, and advocating for the formulation and reformulation of laws on GEWE. WROs have also been playing a key role in holding the government more accountable for domestication of all commitments made and enforcing women’s rights, a case in point being the CEDAW. Women’s NGOs, notably EWLA, Network of Ethiopian Women's Associations (NEWA) and Setaweet have engaged in preparing country shadow reports on CEDAW implementation. providing an alternative source of information and evaluation to the UN monitoring committee.
Other key WROs in Ethiopia include Women Empowerment—Action (WE Action) and Women in Self- Employment (WISE), Yellow Movement, Ethiopian Women with Disability National Association
(EWDNA) and HUNDEE, among others. Following reform to prior restrictive CSO laws, one of the major challenges confronting women rights organizations remains the lack of institutional and technical capacity to deliver on GEWE programmes. Notwithstanding the need for financial support, WROs require skills training in various aspects, including in advocacy, research methodologies, monitoring and documenting human rights, and they also need to network and collaborate with like-minded organizations. They need support to connect themselves to the outside world, more so with respect to relevant international and regional mechanisms to facilitate them effectively engaging with these mechanisms.68 Policy influence at the national level calls for increasing the capacity of WROs to lobby and influence policy formulation, reviews and implementation, strengthening their capacity to support ongoing political reforms, active participation and policy influence in regional and international policy processes, and supporting women's participation in decision-making.
Target for 2021 at 2. Youth led organizations will be identified and participate in capacity trainings and movement building for the whole project period

This will inform further work and priority issues for the organisations that are part of the project.

title.narrative: Number of laws blocked, adopted or improved to promote women’s voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes in public, private and civic sphere.

description.narrative: Laws blocked, adopted or improved to promote women’s voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes in public, private and civic sphere.

comment.narrative: Although Ethiopia is replete with a history of women’s engagement in the public and political spheres and significant progress on gender equality indices ranking 97 Globally, there are some gaps in the legal frameworks guaranteeing the rights of women to economic and political participation such as the Political Parties Registration and Election’s Code of Conduct and the Economic Reform Policy that target vulnerable groups in Ethiopian society, specifically women.
Influence the improvement of the anti-violence and GBV law

The absence of a comprehensive anti-violence law in Ethiopia limits law enforcement’s ability to pursue incidents of violence. Existing legislation is insufficient, with gaps in addressing domestic violence, marital rape, sexual harassment, and acid attacks. These deficiencies hinder the judicial process due to the lack of detailed standard procedures. EWLA has contributed significantly to updating the gender policy, formulating a new GBV prevention and response strategy, and revising the women’s policy. They reviewed the new draft criminal procedure, provided a written statement to the committee on improving gender sensitivity, appeared in Parliament, and presented findings on gaps in the Draft Criminal Procedure Act. Many of their recommendations were incorporated into the secondary draft. Future plans include organizing consultations with stakeholders to discuss the approval process, identify necessary inclusions, and determine the next steps with the Ministry of Planning and Development (MPD) to keep the process moving forward.

At the start of the project in 2021, there was no formal directive on maternity leave for female students. As the project progressed, women's groups and coalitions, empowered by EWLA, identified gaps in existing and new laws and policies. EWLA and other WROs successfully blocked an ineffective draft directive on maternity leave, advocating for supportive policies for pregnant and parenting students. These efforts led to the Ministry of Education recognizing the need for revision and initiating consultation workshops. These workshops involved policymakers, educators, and women’s rights advocates to ensure the new directive is inclusive and supportive. The revised directive, currently being finalized, reflects a more supportive approach for female students balancing education and parenthood. This change is a direct result of the project's advocacy and engagement, with plans including continued monitoring and advocacy to ensure effective implementation and replication of this success across other sectors.

description.narrative: Governmental policies & strategies blocked, adopted or improved to promote women’s voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes in public, private and civic sphere.

comment.narrative: Although Ethiopia is replete with a history of women’s engagement in the public and political spheres and significant progress on gender equality indices ranking 97 Globally, there are some gaps in the legal frameworks guaranteeing the rights os women to economic and political participation, such as the Political Parties Registration and Election’s Code of Conduct and the Economic Reform Policy, that target vulnerable groups in Ethiopian society, specifically women.
Support the drafting of the women's policy as a part of the technical working group

In Ethiopia, the implementation of laws and policies concerning women's rights and gender equality has been fragmented and lacks cohesive enforcement mechanisms. Many regulations are outdated and fail to address current issues faced by women or promote their participation in decision-making processes. The WCW advocacy efforts have engaged in policy advocacy to strengthen women's rights and participation across various levels. A policy paper was presented to the Ministry of Planning and Development on the draft anti-gender-based violence (GBV) Bill, shaping its provisions to ensure comprehensive protection and support for GBV survivors. Policy training sessions conducted in Adama-Oromia and Addis Ababa catalyzed the commencement of the criminal law amendment process and equipped local policymakers to revise outdated statutes. Further, EWLA’s support during the revision of the women's policy and the anti-GBV prevention and protection policy has been instrumental in creating a unified and stronger framework. The project will continue advocacy, monitoring, and engagement with policymakers to sustain and build upon these successes.

comment.narrative: Although no value was set at baseline as a target since Ethiopia is a party to CEDAW and has also signed and ratified the Maputo Protocol in 2018, the project will work toward enhancing the implementation of international agreements to create an environment conducive to women’s full participation in leadership and decision-making processes.

Although no target was set, the project will focus on enhancing the implementation of international agreements to create an environment conducive to women’s full participation in leadership and decision-making processes

The project aimed to enhance the implementation of international agreements to create an environment conducive to women’s full participation in leadership and decision-making processes. Efforts targeted the adoption and improvement of policies to be more inclusive, enforceable, and aligned with international human rights standards. In Ethiopia, EWLA, in collaboration with other CSOs, presented the 7th to 10th shadow period reports to the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, highlighting developments and gaps in women's rights from 2015 to 2023. This presentation emphasized the need for robust measures to protect women's rights and included these perspectives in regional human rights discourse. Similarly, as a technical member of the National Action Plan (NAP) on 'Women, Peace, and Security,' EWLA collaborates with the Prime Minister's Office and the Ministries of Justice and Women and Social Affairs to adopt a comprehensive and actionable strategy. This process promises to align policies with international standards and local needs, showing substantial progress in the policy framework.

description.narrative: Female individuals have strengthened capacity (knowledge and skills) to advance women's rights and gender equality

comment.narrative: The baseline is zero
Target 89 females who have been part of the project during the MTR

From the midterm review conducted in June 2023, out of the 89 WRAs supported by the project under the Ethiopia Women’s Coalition, 30 (34%) of them reported having strengthened advocacy and lobbying skills. For example, in 2023 alone, 30 women participated in policy change advocacy workshops in collaboration with the Ethiopian Women Lawyers Association (EWLA). Their efforts contributed to initiating the criminal law amendment procedure in the region. Similarly, in the Adama-Oromia Region, 30 female trainees worked with the EWLA to campaign against the directive that prohibited pregnant girls from staying in school. During the 16 Days of Activism, their campaign successfully influenced the Ministry of Education to revise the directive, allowing girls to continue their academic year regardless of pregnancy. As a result, a total of 60 women from both regions have demonstrated improved attitudes and practices towards women's voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes.

Summary of Baseline findings: Most of the activists are freelance and engage on issues supported by various organizations. Current leadership status among the participants varied across the countries; Regionally 55(50%), South Sudan 13(93%), Sudan 17(68%), Somaliland 4(57%), Uganda 16 (34%), Somali 2(20%) and Ethiopia 3(38%). Most of these leadership positions are held at the community level. Additionally, at WROs level, the average number of female staff across the countries is 167.5 while that of the male is staff is 23.3. Several women have risen to leadership positions across the surveyed countries. Somaliland had the highest number of women in leadership positions at 34%. This was followed by Ethiopia with 32%. The remaining countries, South Sudan, Sudan Uganda and Somali, had a mean of less than 10% The perception of participants in political affairs was also assessed. Although not very positive across the region except for Uganda, almost half of the participants 39(35%) perceive that the political process is fair for women aspirants; Uganda 27(57.4%), Ethiopia 7(87.5%) while only Somali 1(10%), South Sudan 1(7.1%), and Sudan 1(4.0%) and Somaliland 2(8.6%). Structural conditions limiting women’s participation in decision-making roles include high levels of illiteracy; low levels of education, awareness of women’s rights, and self-esteem; lack of energy/time outside of economic activities; and high rates of VAW/G. Some women face more barriers than others: women from minority clans; internally displaced women and other migrants living in camps and informal urban settlements; poor rural pastoral women; women with disabilities; young women.
